ARCHITECTURE & GOVERNANCE / 02

Intelligence changes
the architecture.

AI models bring new capability to enterprise software. But reliable agentic systems require far more than a capable model.

Scope AI · 31 October 2026 · Updated 2 November 2026 · Architecture perspective

IN THIS ARTICLE

What actually changes?Six dimensionsBusiness authorityA KYC exampleArchitecture before productsOur principlePeople and operational ownership

For decades, enterprise teams have built software around processes, data, rules and integrations. An AI model adds the ability to interpret unfamiliar inputs, reason about a situation, plan a response and select possible actions. That changes the architecture—but does not remove the need for sound software engineering.

The model is a new component, not the whole system.

In a conventional workflow, engineers typically define the paths the application can follow. An agentic workflow can choose among actions based on context, instructions and model outputs. The same request may take different reasoning paths, even when the desired business result is unchanged.

Traditional systems already need identity, security, observability and governance. Agentic systems add new failure modes because a probabilistic reasoning component may influence tool use, sequence of work and proposed decisions.

THE ARCHITECTURAL SHIFT

We are no longer designing only the steps software executes. We are also designing the boundaries within which software may choose its next step.

Six dimensions of an agentic system.

  1. Intelligence. What genuinely requires interpretation or reasoning? What should stay deterministic?
  2. Knowledge and context. Which policies, records and instructions are relevant, authorized, current and traceable?
  3. Orchestration. Who manages workflow state, retries, uncertainty, handoffs and recovery when something fails?
  4. Tools and actions. Which systems may the agent read or change? On whose behalf, and under what conditions?
  5. Containment and security. Which controls must be enforced outside the model—through identities, APIs, permissions, network boundaries and runtime isolation?
  6. Evaluation and assurance. How do we test not only the final answer, but also the decisions, evidence, actions, denials and behavior under attack or uncertainty?

These are architectural responsibilities, not a shopping list. A single product may cover several of them; no single product removes the need to define the business rules.

Business architecture must define the authority first.

Before selecting a framework or a tool gateway, establish the business contract. What outcome matters? Which decisions belong to a human? Which actions may be automated? Which policy defines the exception? What evidence will make the result acceptable?

Agentic business architecture specifies outcomes, process, business rules, decision rights, human checkpoints, data meaning and acceptance criteria. Agentic technical architecture translates that contract into models, orchestration, integrations, enforced permissions, deployment, monitoring and evaluation.

These two views should connect through reviewed specifications, not rely on assumptions passed between teams.

A banking example: prepare a KYC review, do not silently decide it.

Consider a proposed assistant that gathers authorized case records, retrieves current KYC policy and drafts an evidence-linked review summary. The model can help interpret documents and identify missing information.

But the business must specify whether the assistant can only recommend, whether it may update a case, which reviewer approves changes, and what happens when the records conflict. The technical design must then enforce those permissions at the API and identity layer—not merely instruct the model to behave.

A useful evaluation set includes accurate summaries, missing evidence, conflicting policies, unauthorized record requests, attempted writes, prompt injection and tool failures. A plausible narrative is not enough; the system must produce the right result and respect the right boundaries.

This is an illustrative synthetic pilot design, not a deployed banking system or a claim of regulatory compliance.

Own the decisions. Integrate the infrastructure.

Enterprises already have cloud services, identity systems, APIs and operational controls. Specialized products may add tool authorization, runtime isolation or evaluation capabilities. The correct architecture may combine them—or need fewer components than a vendor diagram suggests.

That is why Scope AI takes a vendor-neutral approach: define the business authority and control requirements, compare existing and candidate platforms, record architecture decisions and test the selected design against the same scenarios.

We should not rebuild a governance platform simply because agents are new. Nor should we mistake purchasing one for having solved governance.

The principle behind governed intelligence.

SCOPE AI ARCHITECTURE PRINCIPLE

Intelligence expands what software can decide. Architecture determines what it is allowed to do. Evaluation determines whether we can trust the outcome.

The important question is not simply, “How intelligent is the model?” It is, “Can this whole system deliver a valuable business outcome while respecting authority, evidence and operational constraints?”

That is the shift from experimenting with a model to engineering an enterprise agentic system.

Design the work people will actually own.

A workflow changes the responsibilities of the people around it. Before building, listen to the case preparer, reviewer and service owner. Establish which burden should improve, which decisions must remain theirs, and how they can correct or challenge an output.

Strong ground means an agreed purpose, clear commitments and honest treatment of uncertainty. The practical support includes review time, training, escalation routes, recovery procedures and ownership after launch. A technically successful deployment can still fail if the team cannot operate it.

Start with a bounded pilot, compare outcomes with a baseline, and examine both system behaviour and people's workload. Use existing delivery gates to review readiness and evidence. Expand when the results and support arrangements justify it.
